blocks.text: A healthy 27-year-old at 30 weeks reports that she feels breathless climbing stairs, her ankles are swollen and she is dizzy when she stands quickly. Her haemoglobin is 108 g/L, her serum creatinine is lower than it was before pregnancy and her pulse is 92. Every one of these findings is normal for her. Before you can recognise disease in pregnancy, you must know what normal looks like.

blocks.markdown: Pregnancy is a state of sustained physiological stress in which almost every maternal organ system adapts to supply the placenta and fetus. The changes are driven by **progesterone and oestrogen** (vasodilation, smooth muscle relaxation, fluid retention), by **placental hormones** and by the demand for blood flow through the uteroplacental circulation, which at term receives about 500 to 700 mL per minute.

blocks.title: Cardiac output
blocks.text: Cardiac output is the volume of blood the heart pumps per minute: cardiac output = heart rate x stroke volume. In pregnancy it rises by about 30 to 50 percent, reaching a plateau by roughly 28 to 32 weeks, through a rise in both heart rate (by about 10 to 20 beats per minute) and stroke volume.

blocks.caption: Cardiac output (mL per min) equals heart rate (beats per min) multiplied by stroke volume (mL per beat).

blocks.markdown:
**Cardiovascular adaptations.** Systemic vascular resistance falls because progesterone and nitric oxide dilate vessels and the low-resistance placenta is added to the circuit. Blood pressure therefore *falls* in early pregnancy, reaching a nadir in the second trimester (about 20 to 24 weeks) and returning toward pre-pregnancy levels by term. Plasma volume expands by about 40 to 50 percent, so there is a mild fall in jugular venous pressure and a flow murmur is common. After about 20 weeks, lying supine allows the gravid uterus to compress the inferior vena cava and reduce venous return, causing **supine hypotensive syndrome**, relieved by left lateral tilt.

**Haematological adaptations.** Plasma volume rises by 40 to 50 percent while red cell mass rises by about 20 to 30 percent, so haemoglobin concentration and haematocrit fall, the **physiological anaemia of pregnancy** (haemoglobin nadir around 32 weeks). White cell count rises, platelets fall slightly, and the coagulation system becomes **hypercoagulable** (raised fibrinogen and factors VII, VIII and X, reduced fibrinolysis), which protects against haemorrhage at delivery but increases the risk of venous thromboembolism.

**Renal adaptations.** Renal plasma flow and **glomerular filtration rate (GFR) rise by about 50 percent** early in pregnancy. Serum creatinine and urea therefore *fall*, so a creatinine value that is normal outside pregnancy may be abnormal in pregnancy. The collecting system dilates (hydroureter and hydronephrosis, right more than left) because of progesterone and compression by the uterus, predisposing to urinary infection. Glycosuria is common because filtered glucose exceeds tubular reabsorption.

Fall in systemic vascular resistance; rise in heart rate and stroke volume
Plasma volume up 40 to 50 percent; red cell mass up 20 to 30 percent; hypercoagulable
GFR up about 50 percent; ureteric dilatation
Increased renal plasma flow; progesterone smooth muscle relaxation
Low creatinine; glycosuria; urinary infection risk
Tidal volume up; mild respiratory alkalosis
blocks.caption: Maternal adaptations to pregnancy.

blocks.title: How dilution lowers haemoglobin
blocks.prompt: Before pregnancy a woman has plasma volume 2.6 L, red cell volume 1.4 L and haemoglobin 130 g/L. In late pregnancy plasma volume rises by 45 percent and red cell volume by 20 percent, with no change in the haemoglobin per red cell. Estimate her haematocrit and haemoglobin concentration.

steps.text: Haematocrit is red cell volume divided by total blood volume; compare with before (1.4 / 4.0 = 35 percent).
Haemoglobin concentration scales with red cell volume divided by total volume, so it falls by the same ratio as the haematocrit.

blocks.answer: Haematocrit about 31 percent and haemoglobin about 114 g/L: a fall caused by dilution, not by loss of red cells.

blocks.markdown:
**Taking an obstetric history.** Record the **last menstrual period (LMP)** and whether it was certain and normal, cycle length and regularity, contraceptive use, and details of every previous pregnancy (gestation, mode of delivery, birth weight, complications), then medical, surgical, drug, family and social history. **Gravidity** (G) is the number of pregnancies including the present one; **parity** (P) is the number of births at or after 24 weeks (UK); losses before 24 weeks are noted after a plus sign. A woman who is currently pregnant and has had two term births and one miscarriage at 9 weeks is G4 P2+1.

**Calculating the expected date of delivery (EDD).** For a woman with a regular 28-day cycle, **Naegele's rule** adds 1 year, subtracts 3 months and adds 7 days to the first day of the LMP (equivalently 280 days or 40 weeks). Cycles longer or shorter than 28 days shift ovulation, so add or subtract the difference. Gestational age by dates is the interval from the LMP. Ultrasound dating by crown-rump length (about 11+2 to 14+1 weeks) is used when the LMP is uncertain, and in the UK the scan date replaces the LMP date when they differ by more than about 7 days.

blocks.title: Calculating an EDD with a long cycle
blocks.prompt: A woman's LMP started on 14 August 2025. Her cycles are regular at 32 days. Calculate her EDD.

steps.text: Apply Naegele's rule: add 1 year, subtract 3 months, add 7 days.
Adjust for the cycle: her cycle is 32 days, which is 4 days longer than 28, so ovulation is delayed by about 4 days and the EDD moves 4 days later.
State gestational age in the same way: weeks and days measured from the LMP, adjusted if the cycle is not 28 days.

blocks.markdown: **The booking visit.** The booking visit should take place ideally by 10 weeks. It consists of a full history and examination, measurement of blood pressure, weight and BMI, urinalysis, and a risk assessment. Routine screening offered at booking in the UK includes: **full blood count** (anaemia), **blood group, rhesus D status and red cell antibodies**, **haemoglobinopathy screening** (sickle cell disease and thalassaemia), **infection screening for HIV, hepatitis B and syphilis**, **midstream urine culture** (asymptomatic bacteriuria), and **offer of screening for Down, Edwards and Patau syndromes** with the dating scan. A woman is also assessed for gestational diabetes risk, venous thromboembolism risk, mental health, domestic abuse, smoking and alcohol, and receives advice on folic acid, vitamin D, diet and vaccination. All screening is by informed consent.

items: Cardiac output rises 30 to 50 percent; blood pressure dips in the second trimester.
Plasma volume rises more than red cell mass, giving physiological anaemia.
GFR rises by about 50 percent, so creatinine falls.
EDD is LMP plus 280 days (Naegele's rule), adjusted for cycle length and ultrasound dating.
Booking tests: FBC, blood group and antibodies, haemoglobinopathies, HIV, hepatitis B, syphilis, urine culture.

blocks.title: Reference ranges move in pregnancy
blocks.text: Always interpret creatinine, haemoglobin and blood pressure against pregnancy-specific expectations. A creatinine that would be reassuring in a non-pregnant adult can signal renal impairment in pregnancy, and a haemoglobin that looks only mildly low may be physiologically normal.

points: Cardiac output rises 30 to 50 percent while systemic vascular resistance and blood pressure fall in the second trimester.
Plasma volume increases more than red cell mass, producing physiological anaemia; coagulation is hypercoagulable and GFR rises about 50 percent.
Gravidity counts all pregnancies; parity counts births from 24 weeks; EDD uses Naegele's rule with adjustment for cycle length and scan dating.
The booking visit offers blood count, blood group and antibodies, haemoglobinopathy and infection screening, urine culture and risk assessment.

questions.stem: Which of the following changes is normal in healthy pregnancy?

distractorRationale.a: Correct: progesterone, nitric oxide and the placental circuit reduce resistance.
distractorRationale.c: Plasma volume rises by 40 to 50 percent.

questions.explanation: Vasodilation lowers systemic vascular resistance, which accounts for the mid-pregnancy fall in blood pressure. The other options are the opposite of the normal changes in plasma volume, GFR and creatinine.

questions.stem: A woman at 28 weeks has a serum creatinine of 85 micromoles per litre. Her pre-pregnancy value was 68 micromoles per litre. Which interpretation is most appropriate?

options.text: Normal, because values within the non-pregnant range need no further review
Concerning, because GFR normally rises in pregnancy and creatinine should fall, so a rise suggests impaired renal function
Expected, because GFR falls in pregnancy

questions.correctOptionText: Concerning, because GFR normally rises in pregnancy and creatinine should fall, so a rise suggests impaired renal function

distractorRationale.a: Pregnancy-specific values are lower, so this is abnormal.

questions.explanation: A 50 percent rise in GFR lowers creatinine in pregnancy, so a rise from a low baseline is not normal. It warrants assessment for renal disease or pre-eclampsia.

questions.stem: A woman at 12 weeks has had two previous term deliveries, one termination at 8 weeks and one miscarriage at 11 weeks. How is her obstetric status recorded using the UK convention?

distractorRationale.a: Gravidity must include the current pregnancy: 2 births plus 2 losses plus now is 5.
distractorRationale.c: Losses before 24 weeks are not counted in parity.
distractorRationale.d: This omits the losses and the current pregnancy.

questions.explanation: Gravidity counts every pregnancy including the present one, giving 2 plus 2 plus 1, which equals 5. Parity counts births at or after 24 weeks (2), and the two early losses are added after the plus sign.

questions.stem: Which infections are routinely screened for at the antenatal booking visit in the UK?

distractorRationale.a: Correct: these are offered to all women with consent.
distractorRationale.b: Not routine at booking in the UK.
distractorRationale.d: Not part of routine UK screening.

questions.explanation: HIV, hepatitis B and syphilis can be transmitted to the baby and are treatable or preventable, so universal screening is offered at booking. Screening is voluntary and requires informed consent.

questions.stem: A woman at booking is found to be rhesus D negative with no red cell antibodies. What is the main reason for including blood group and antibody screen at booking?

options.text: To prevent and detect rhesus alloimmunisation, which can cause haemolytic disease of the fetus and newborn
To determine the sex of the baby

questions.correctOptionText: To prevent and detect rhesus alloimmunisation, which can cause haemolytic disease of the fetus and newborn

distractorRationale.a: Correct: rhesus negative women are offered anti-D prophylaxis at sensitising events and antibodies are monitored.
distractorRationale.b: Blood group does not predict pre-eclampsia.
distractorRationale.c: Blood group is unrelated to glucose.
distractorRationale.d: Not the purpose of the test.

questions.explanation: If an RhD-negative woman carries an RhD-positive fetus she can form antibodies that cross the placenta and cause haemolysis in later pregnancies. Identifying her status early allows prophylactic anti-D and surveillance.

questions.stem: True or false: Naegele's rule, which adds 1 year, subtracts 3 months and adds 7 days to the LMP, assumes a regular 28-day menstrual cycle.
questions.explanation: The rule is equivalent to adding 280 days, which assumes ovulation on day 14 of a 28-day cycle. For longer or shorter cycles the EDD is adjusted by the difference from 28 days.

questions.stem: A woman at 30 weeks has a heart rate of 88 beats per minute and a stroke volume of 85 mL per beat. Calculate her cardiac output in litres per minute (to one decimal place).
questions.explanation: Cardiac output equals heart rate multiplied by stroke volume, 88 times 85, which is 7480 mL per minute, or about 7.5 L per minute. This is about 50 percent higher than a typical non-pregnant value of around 5 L per minute.

questions.stem: A woman with a certain LMP of 3 January 2026 and a regular 28-day cycle attends on 28 March 2026. How many completed weeks of gestation does she have by dates?
questions.explanation: From 3 January to 28 March is 28 days remaining in January, 28 in February and 28 in March, giving 84 days. Dividing by 7 gives exactly 12 completed weeks.

questions.stem: Explain the haematological adaptations of pregnancy, including why haemoglobin concentration falls and why pregnant women are at increased risk of venous thromboembolism.
markingGuide: Plasma volume rises by about 40 to 50 percent
Red cell mass rises by about 20 to 30 percent, a proportionally smaller increase
Dilution lowers haemoglobin concentration and haematocrit: physiological anaemia with nadir about 32 weeks
Anaemia defined by trimester-specific thresholds so true iron deficiency is not missed
Hypercoagulable state: increased fibrinogen and factors VII, VIII and X, reduced fibrinolysis
Benefit: reduces haemorrhage at delivery; risk: venous thromboembolism, aggravated by venous stasis from compression by the uterus
Leucocytosis and mild fall in platelet count
questions.explanation: Haematological changes serve the dual purpose of perfusing the placenta and protecting against delivery blood loss. The same changes explain physiological anaemia and the higher thrombosis risk.

questions.stem: Describe the routine investigations and screening offered at the antenatal booking visit, and explain why each is included.
markingGuide: Blood pressure, BMI and urinalysis for baseline and risk assessment
Full blood count to detect anaemia
Blood group, rhesus D status and red cell antibodies to prevent haemolytic disease
Haemoglobinopathy screening (sickle cell, thalassaemia) for the mother and, if positive, the partner
HIV, hepatitis B and syphilis screening to allow treatment and prevention of vertical transmission
Midstream urine culture for asymptomatic bacteriuria
Offer of screening for Down, Edwards and Patau syndromes with the dating scan, by informed consent
Risk assessments for gestational diabetes, venous thromboembolism, mental health, domestic abuse and substance use; folic acid and vitamin D advice
questions.explanation: Each test identifies a condition that is treatable or modifiable and that threatens mother or fetus if missed. All screening is offered with counselling and informed consent.
